claims.text: Sharing electrons is the defining covalent mechanism. Ionic bonding instead emphasizes oppositely charged ions and electrostatic attraction.
Directional differences in bond strength permit cleavage. The weakest recurring plane can separate while stronger bonds within each sheet remain intact.
Gypsum is a sulfate, while pyrite is a sulfide. Sharing one element does not make minerals members of the same chemical family.
Calcite is a carbonate, halite a halide, and magnetite an oxide. The other sets include silicon–oxygen tetrahedral minerals.
Granite and rhyolite share felsic composition but differ in texture and cooling history. Composition and texture are independent classification axes.

lesson.title: Why Rock Melts—and Why Magma Flows
body: Hot does not automatically mean molten. Much of the mantle remains solid because temperature must be compared with the melting boundary at that pressure. The geothermal gradient describes how temperature varies with depth; it is not itself the melting curve.

Three routes promote melting: add heat, lower pressure while material rises (decompression), or add water/volatiles that lower the melting temperature. Water does not have to heat the rock or reduce its pressure to cause melting. In a diagram, identify which condition changes and how it crosses the solidus.

Viscosity is resistance to flow. Higher temperature generally lowers magma viscosity; more silica generally increases it by promoting linked structures. Dissolved water generally lowers viscosity, whereas a higher crystal load generally raises it. Apply one-variable comparisons rather than treating viscosity as another word for density.
keyPoints: Cross the melting boundary by changing temperature, pressure, or composition.
Hotter generally flows more easily; more silica or crystals generally resists flow.

lesson.title: Bowen and Changing Magma Composition
body: Bowen’s reaction series connects cooling to mineral sequence. On the discontinuous branch: olivine → pyroxene → amphibole → biotite. Plagioclase changes from calcium-rich toward sodium-rich on the continuous branch. Potassium feldspar, muscovite, and quartz are characteristic late, lower-temperature minerals.

The sequence is not a requirement that every magma produce every mineral. Composition and conditions matter. The 1001-level target is early mafic versus late felsic minerals, plus recognition of the two branches—not memorizing a universal exact crystallization temperature.

Partial melting need not produce a melt identical to its source. Crystal separation can remove early mafic minerals, leaving residual melt relatively silica-rich. Assimilation incorporates surrounding rock; magma mixing combines magmas. Keep these mechanisms separate: sorting crystals is not the same as melting wall rock.
keyPoints: Early olivine/pyroxene contrasts with late quartz/K-feldspar/muscovite.
Crystal separation, assimilation, and mixing are different mechanisms.

lesson.title: Secondary: Settings and Intrusive Shapes
body: Secondary review: these topics appear in the supplied quiz and textbook, but their exam weight is unknown. Finish the chart and core cause-and-effect modules first. This section is not a claim that every geographic example will be examined.

Mid-ocean ridges commonly produce basalt at the surface and gabbro at depth. At subduction zones, water released from a descending slab promotes melting in the overlying mantle. Magma interacting with thick continental crust can evolve toward intermediate or felsic composition. Oceanic hot spots commonly produce basalt; continental settings can include more evolved melts.

A dike cuts across existing layering; a sill intrudes parallel to it. A laccolith domes overlying layers. A volcanic neck occupies a former conduit; a batholith is a large intrusive body. Columnar joints form as hot solid rock cools and contracts. Calderas involve collapse associated with magma withdrawal; do not confuse them with intrusive bodies.
keyPoints: Setting helps constrain composition; crustal interaction can modify magma.
Cross-cutting dike; parallel sill; doming laccolith; contraction joints.

Plagioclase changes from calcium-rich toward sodium-rich on the continuous branch. Potassium feldspar, muscovite, and quartz are characteristic late, lower-temperature minerals.

The sequence is not a requirement that every magma produce every mineral. Composition and conditions matter. The 1001-level target is early mafic versus late felsic minerals, plus recognition of the two branches—not memorizing a universal exact crystallization temperature.

Partial melting need not produce a melt identical to its source. Crystal separation can remove early mafic minerals, leaving residual melt relatively silica-rich. Assimilation incorporates surrounding rock; magma mixing combines magmas. Keep these mechanisms separate: sorting crystals is not the same as melting wall rock.

concepts.label: Tectonic setting and magma
concepts.teaching:
Secondary review: these topics appear in the supplied quiz and textbook, but their exam weight is unknown. Finish the chart and core cause-and-effect modules first. This section is not a claim that every geographic example will be examined.

Mid-ocean ridges commonly produce basalt at the surface and gabbro at depth. At subduction zones, water released from a descending slab promotes melting in the overlying mantle. Magma interacting with thick continental crust can evolve toward intermediate or felsic composition. Oceanic hot spots commonly produce basalt; continental settings can include more evolved melts.

A dike cuts across existing layering; a sill intrudes parallel to it. A laccolith domes overlying layers. A volcanic neck occupies a former conduit; a batholith is a large intrusive body. Columnar joints form as hot solid rock cools and contracts. Calderas involve collapse associated with magma withdrawal; do not confuse them with intrusive bodies.

gradedItems.prompt: An atomic model emphasizes electrons shared between adjacent atoms. Which bond mechanism is being illustrated?
gradedItems.explanation: Sharing electrons is the defining covalent mechanism. Ionic bonding instead emphasizes oppositely charged ions and electrostatic attraction.

gradedItems.prompt: Why can a mineral be strongly bonded within a sheet yet split easily into sheets?
choices: Strong bonds mean cleavage is impossible
Every bond must be equally weak
Bonds between the sheets are weaker than bonds within them
The mineral must melt before splitting
gradedItems.explanation: Directional differences in bond strength permit cleavage. The weakest recurring plane can separate while stronger bonds within each sheet remain intact.
gradedItems.hint: Focus on what the electrons do.

gradedItems.prompt: A student groups gypsum with pyrite because both contain sulfur. What distinction was missed?

gradedItems.hint: Look for the defining chemical group, not a similar-sounding name.

gradedItems.prompt: Which set contains only nonsilicate minerals?
gradedItems.explanation: Calcite is a carbonate, halite a halide, and magnetite an oxide. The other sets include silicon–oxygen tetrahedral minerals.

gradedItems.prompt: An igneous sheet crosses several sedimentary layers at a steep angle. Which geometric relationship identifies it?
choices: It is necessarily a sill because it is thin
It is a clast because layers are present
It is a dike because it cuts across layering
gradedItems.explanation: A dike cuts across pre-existing structure. A sill follows layering; its identity is relational, not simply whether it appears horizontal in a picture.
gradedItems.hint: Use relationships to the host layers, not just vertical versus horizontal on the page.
